newsitem.title: USA: Army probes sex charges against top enlisted man.
newsitem.headline: Army probes sex charges against top enlisted man.

text.p: The U.S. Army said on Tuesday that its top enlisted man will remain on duty at the Pentagon while it investigates "serious" charges of sexual harassment against him by a retired female soldier.
Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney denied that he accosted a female sergeant major in a hotel in Hawaii last year and remained on the job as the top enlisted adviser to senior Army leadership.
But McKinney asked to be relieved of his duties on a panel reviewing sexual harassment policies in the service.

It was the latest allegation in a scandal which began last November when male trainers at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground training centre in Maryland were charged with harassing and even raping female recruits.

"We consider this set of allegations serious, just as any other set of allegations that have been received since November," said Major Joe Piek, an Army spokesman at the Pentagon. "He (McKinney) is continuing his duties as sergeant major of the Army."

The Army said a 13-page document of allegations by Brenda Hoster, a 22-year veteran who retired last year after reaching the rank of sergeant major, had been turned over to the service's Criminal Investigative Division (CID).

The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Hoster said in an interview that McKinney had grabbed and kissed her in a hotel room in Hawaii last April, but had left when she rejected his sexual advances.
His wife was in a room just down the hall at the time, Hoster said in the interview, according to the Times.

Army officials said the service learned of the allegations on Monday and that the CID had immediately launched an investigation of McKinney, who has a Pentagon office directly across from the Army chief of staff, Gen. Dennis Reimer.
McKinney "denies he ever engaged in any form of sexual misconduct or improper treatment with the retired sergeant major who made the allegations," the Army said in a statement.
Hoster told the Times that she had decided to leave the service last August partly "for the good of the Army" and partly because she feared that no one would believe her if she pressed her case.
But she said that she decided she could no longer remain silent when Army Secretary Togo West appointed McKinney, 46, to a senior panel gathered to investigate sexual harassment in the service.
Six instructors and trainers at Aberdeen have been charged in a sexual harassment scandal that erupted last November. The scandal has also spread to other bases.
